summary: Specifies a minimal YANG data model for TCP on devices managed through network management protocols. It defines a container for all TCP connections and reusable groupings for authentication parameters, which other models can import when they need to configure TCP.

eli5.summary: TCP is how computers keep a steady conversation going. This gives a simple standard list of the knobs and dials on that conversation so management software can see and set them.

subtitle: A small, reusable YANG model for configuring and monitoring TCP on routers and other managed devices.

tldr.problem: Network devices are configured through YANG-based protocols such as NETCONF and RESTCONF, but there was no standard YANG model for basic TCP settings, TCP authentication or TCP statistics.
tldr.mechanism: The ietf-tcp module defines a tcp container with a list of connections, a list of listeners and a set of statistics, plus reusable groupings and an augmentation of the key chain model for TCP-AO and MD5 authentication.
tldr.outcome: The model is deliberately minimal, covering fundamental TCP functions that other models can import and extend. It does not deprecate the TCP MIB.

facts.label: Connection key
facts.value: local address, remote address, local port, remote port

today: RFC 9648 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2024, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines the initial version of the module, and the text expects it to be augmented or updated for more advanced TCP features.

sections.title: Why TCP Needs a YANG Model
sections.content:
TCP (RFC 9293) runs on many network elements that are configured and managed through protocols such as NETCONF (RFC 6241) and RESTCONF (RFC 8040). RFC 9648 specifies a minimal YANG 1.1 data model for configuring and managing TCP on such devices.

The model contains a TCP connection table, a TCP listener table and an augmentation of the YANG key chain model (RFC 8177) to support authentication. It is compliant with the Network Management Datastore Architecture (NMDA).

Its scope is narrow on purpose: a subset of fundamental TCP functions and basic statistics. The module can be augmented or updated later for more advanced or implementation-specific features.
sections.eli5: Routers are managed by software, and that software needs a common language for talking about TCP. This document is a small dictionary of that language.

sections.title: Scope and What Is Left Out
sections.content:
TCP is implemented in many different ways, and settings can live at different levels: system-wide (for example, turning window scaling on or off), per interface (for example, the Maximum Segment Size), per connection (for example, socket options such as TCP_NODELAY) or in application preferences. The RFC notes that there is no ground truth for where a given parameter belongs, and different systems use different defaults.

The model therefore keeps to a minimal set of fundamental parameters that matter on network elements such as routers. It does not model details of Multipath TCP (RFC 8684), and it does not cover the TCP extended statistics MIB (RFC 4898).

The module also leaves out some parameters from the TCP MIB, most notably Retransmission Timeout (RTO) configuration and a maximum connection limit. The authors call this a conscious decision, because these parameters hardly matter in a state-of-the-art TCP implementation.

This specification does not deprecate the TCP MIB (RFC 4022). The basic statistics follow the model of that MIB, but the RFC chose not to machine-translate the MIB into YANG because the result would not be up to date.
sections.eli5: The authors only listed the settings that really matter and left out the rest, like packing only the things you will use on a trip.

sections.title: Structure of the Model
sections.content:
The module ietf-tcp has a top-level tcp container. Inside it are three parts:

  • connections: a list of TCP connections, identified by the four values local address, remote address, local port and remote port. Each entry can carry a desired mss (Maximum Segment Size), a pmtud switch for Path MTU Discovery (default false), the keepalive settings pulled in from RFC 9643, and a read-only state.
  • tcp-listeners: a read-only list of listeners, meaning applications willing to accept connections, keyed by address type, address and port.
  • statistics: read-only counters, available when the statistics feature is supported.

The model reuses definitions from "YANG Groupings for TCP Clients and TCP Servers" (RFC 9643), and it defines groupings so that other YANG models can import them as part of a protocol-specific stack, such as a BGP model.

The connection list is writable even though a connection cannot be created simply by adding an entry. Only some nodes, such as keepalives, are really writable, and what happens when an entry is removed is implementation-specific. The state leaf uses values closed (1) through time-wait (11), and connections in the CLOSED state may not appear in the list.
sections.eli5: There is a big folder called tcp. Inside it is a list of conversations that are happening, a list of doors that are waiting for visitors, and a scoreboard of totals.

sections.title: Statistics and the Reset Action
sections.content:
Like the TCP MIB, the model defines basic counters. They include active-opens, passive-opens, attempt-fails, establish-resets, in-segments, out-segments, retransmitted-segments, in-errors and out-resets. Most are 64-bit counters. currently-established is a 32-bit gauge. When the authentication feature is supported there is also auth-failures, which counts failures with either TCP-AO or MD5.

The model adds one thing the TCP MIB lacks: a reset action that clears the statistics. It takes an optional reset-at time and returns a reset-finished-at time. The RFC says this is not a major addition, because a reset can be implemented by storing offset values for the counters. The action is marked nacm:default-deny-all, so access control must explicitly allow it.
sections.eli5: The scoreboard counts things like how many conversations started and how many failed. There is also a button to wipe the scoreboard back to zero, but only trusted people may press it.

sections.title: TCP Authentication Configuration
sections.content:
The model augments the key chain model with an authentication container, available under the authentication feature. It holds a reference to a key chain and a choice between two methods: TCP-AO (RFC 5925) and the legacy TCP MD5 signature option (RFC 2385).

The TCP-AO grouping has these settings: send-id and recv-id (the KeyIDs sent and matched, which should mirror each other at the two ends), include-tcp-options (default true), accept-key-mismatch and a read-only r-next-key-id. An identity aes-128 names the AES128 algorithm used by TCP-AO.

MD5 is supported to accommodate the installed base, notably BGP deployments. The RFC says it is RECOMMENDED to use TCP-AO, because the MD5 option was obsoleted by TCP-AO in 2010.
sections.eli5: Two computers can agree on a secret handshake so they know they are really talking to each other. The model lets you choose the newer handshake or the older one, but it says to prefer the newer.

sections.title: Worked Configuration Examples
sections.content:
Appendix A gives two XML examples. The first configures one connection from 192.0.2.1 port 1025 to 192.0.2.2 port 22, with mss 1400, pmtud on, and keepalives with idle-time 5, max-probes 5 and probe-interval 10. According to the example's comment, an idle connection is dropped after idle-time + (max-probes * probe-interval).

The second shows a key chain named ao-config with key-id 55, using the tcp:aes-128 algorithm, with TCP-AO send-id 61 and recv-id 84. Its values are taken from the TCP-AO test vectors in RFC 9235.
sections.eli5: The examples show what filling in the form looks like: one for how long to wait before checking a quiet connection is still alive, and one for setting up the secret handshake.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The module is accessed through YANG-based protocols such as NETCONF and RESTCONF, which have mandatory-to-implement secure transports and mutual authentication. The Network Configuration Access Control Model (NACM, RFC 8341) can restrict users to a subset of operations and content.

Writable nodes are sensitive. Unrestricted access to the common configuration, such as the keepalive idle timer, can make connections fail or time out prematurely. Unrestricted access to authentication configuration can prevent authenticated communication and cause connection setups to fail.

Readable nodes are sensitive too: unrestricted access to connection information or statistics can help a malicious user launch an attack. The reset action should be restricted to users with the right permission. Finally, MD5 suffers from the weaknesses discussed in RFC 6151 and RFC 6952.
sections.eli5: The settings and the scoreboard should only be touched by the right people. Letting anyone change them could break connections or help an attacker.

viz.caption: ABRIDGED TREE OF THE ietf-tcp MODULE (RFC 9648)

children.label: connection
children.note: keyed by local/remote address and port

viz.caption: VALUES OF THE CONNECTION STATE LEAF

items.label: closed
items.desc: Connection is closed; may not appear in the list.

items.label: listen
items.desc: Waiting for a connection request from any remote peer and port.

items.label: syn-sent
items.desc: Waiting for a matching request after sending one.

items.label: syn-received
items.desc: Waiting for a confirming acknowledgment after both sending and receiving a request.

items.label: established
items.desc: Open connection; the normal data transfer state.

items.label: fin-wait-1
items.desc: Waiting for a termination request or the acknowledgment of one already sent.

items.label: fin-wait-2
items.desc: Waiting for a termination request from the remote peer.

items.label: close-wait
items.desc: Waiting for a termination request from the local user.

items.label: last-ack
items.desc: Waiting for the acknowledgment of the termination request previously sent.

items.label: closing
items.desc: Waiting for a termination acknowledgment from the remote peer.

items.label: time-wait
items.desc: Waiting long enough to be sure the peer received the acknowledgment.
